name: Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract

reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
clinicalPearls: CAKUT is an umbrella term for a spectrum of developmental malformations of the kidneys, collecting systems, bladder and urethra, and is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease in children

It includes renal agenesis, hypoplasia and dysplasia, multicystic dysplastic kidney, duplex systems, pelvi-ureteric and vesico-ureteric junction obstruction, vesicoureteric reflux and posterior urethral valves
Many cases are detected on antenatal ultrasound as hydronephrosis or abnormal renal appearance, prompting postnatal evaluation

It can be isolated or part of a syndrome; monogenic causes and copy-number variants (for example involving HNF1B or PAX2) are increasingly recognised, and HNF1B disease may be associated with abnormal glucose metabolism and electrolyte disturbance
Posterior urethral valves in males cause bladder outlet obstruction and are an important, potentially treatable cause of obstructive uropathy
Reduced functioning nephron mass predisposes to hypertension, proteinuria and progressive kidney disease over time
Management is largely supportive and urological, with relief of obstruction, prevention and treatment of urinary infection, and long-term surveillance of blood pressure and kidney function
reference.pathophysiology: CAKUT arises from disruption of the tightly orchestrated developmental interactions between the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme that form the kidney and drainage system during embryogenesis. Abnormal budding, branching, nephron induction or lower-tract development produces the wide morphological spectrum, from complete absence or dysplasia of a kidney to obstruction and reflux within the collecting system and bladder outlet. Genetic factors (single-gene variants such as HNF1B and PAX2, and chromosomal copy-number changes) together with environmental influences during nephrogenesis contribute to the phenotype. A reduced or maldeveloped nephron endowment lowers renal functional reserve, so affected individuals are prone to hypertension, proteinuria and gradual decline in glomerular filtration, while obstruction and reflux add risk of infection and further parenchymal injury.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive or dominant polycystic kidney disease
Syndromic disorders with renal involvement (e.g. branchio-oto-renal syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Renal tract ultrasound to define structural anatomy and hydronephrosis
Micturating cystourethrogram to assess reflux and posterior urethral valves
Functional renography (e.g. isotope scanning) to quantify differential function and drainage
Serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate, with urinalysis for proteinuria
Genetic and chromosomal testing (including HNF1B and PAX2) when syndromic or familial disease is suspected
redFlags: Bladder outlet obstruction from posterior urethral valves in a newborn male
Oligohydramnios with pulmonary hypoplasia in severe bilateral disease
Recurrent or febrile urinary tract infections with scarring
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies enormously with the type and severity of the anomaly and the amount of functioning renal tissue; many children do well with monitoring, but bilateral dysplasia, severe obstruction or extensive scarring can progress to chronic and end-stage kidney disease, so lifelong follow-up of blood pressure, proteinuria and renal function is important.
pitfalls: Failing to arrange timely postnatal follow-up of an antenatally detected renal abnormality
Missing posterior urethral valves in a male infant with poor urinary stream or bladder distension
Underestimating the long-term risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease from reduced nephron mass
Overlooking associated extrarenal or syndromic features and the yield of genetic testing (e.g. HNF1B)
Neglecting prevention and prompt treatment of urinary tract infection in refluxing or obstructed systems
references: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology (Feehally, Floege, Tonelli, Johnson)
Oxford Handbook of Nephrology and Hypertension
management: Relieve obstruction surgically according to lesion, with endoscopic ablation of posterior urethral valves, pyeloplasty for pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction and ureteric reimplantation for vesico-ureteric obstruction or reflux
Prevent and promptly treat urinary tract infections, using antibiotic prophylaxis in significant reflux or obstruction
Control blood pressure and reduce proteinuria with renin-angiotensin system blockade such as ACE inhibitors
Manage lower urinary tract dysfunction with bladder training, anticholinergics or clean intermittent catheterisation as needed
Monitor renal function, growth, blood pressure and proteinuria given reduced nephron mass, with conservative chronic kidney disease care and nutritional support
Provide renal replacement therapy by dialysis or transplantation for progression to end-stage kidney disease
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric nephrology and urology follow-up
Offer genetic counselling and family evaluation where monogenic or syndromic disease such as HNF1B or PAX2 is identified

nodes.text: Suspected congenital renal and urinary tract anomaly: hydronephrosis or reflux
Red flag present (posterior urethral valves, oligohydramnios, declining function)?
Urgent urology and nephrology review; relieve bladder outlet obstruction
Renal ultrasound; cystourethrogram; renography; creatinine and eGFR; genetics
Does imaging confirm reflux or obstruction with reduced function?
Consider polycystic disease, ciliopathy or acquired uropathy
Relieve obstruction; endoscopic ablation of posterior urethral valves
Antibiotic prophylaxis for significant reflux or obstruction
ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria and blood pressure
Monitor renal function and growth; dialysis or transplant if progressing
Outcome varies with anomaly type and amount of functioning renal tissue
